articles.summary: Business Center How to Build a Payroll Policy in Nigeria: A Practical Guide for Employers Oluwakemi Adesina August 18, 2026 When setting up a clear payroll policy in Nigeria, you need clear rules on everything from tax laws to staff complaints before anyone gets paid. Relying on inconsistent payroll procedures causes problems quickly: You calculate allowances differently every month, and employees notice. You guess your payment timelines, miss tax deadlines, and get hit with heavy fines. You don’t lock down your data, private salaries leak, and team trust is ruined. This guide changes that. It is a simple map to help you build an accurate system that keeps your HR and finance teams on the exact same page. What Is a Payroll Policy? A company payroll policy is your business playbook for employee pay. It sets the rules for when people get paid, how bonuses are paid, which taxes you must legally deduct, and how you protect private staff data. Do not confuse a policy with a procedure. Your payroll management policy sets the big ground rules, while your monthly procedures are the specific technical steps your team takes to run the numbers. Your HR and finance leaders must build this together. HR makes sure the rules are fair and match local labor habits, while finance ensures the final bill fits your budget and banking limits. What Should a Payroll Policy Include? To build a practical payroll policy template that Nigerian business managers can actually use every month, your document must clearly cover these seven areas: Payday schedule: Pick the exact day your team gets paid (like the 25th of the month). Payroll cut-off dates: Set a hard monthly deadline (like the 18th) to stop taking new overtime logs or expense claims for that cycle. New hire data rules: List what documents a new hire must submit (like their bank details and TIN) before they can join the pay run. Allowances and bonuses: Be clear about how you handle transport, housing, or 13th-month bonuses. Overtime guidelines: Define who qualifies for extra hours and exactly how those rates are calculated. Deductions: List everything that comes out of a paycheck, from government taxes to staff loan repayments. Error fixes: Give your employees a clear, calm way to flag and fix salary mistakes, just in case it happens. Setting Payroll Roles and Approval Controls Depending on your business size, one person should not handle the entire pay run, while a shared password can compromise your payroll system. If the same person types the numbers and sends the payment, you risk mistakes, and when several people have access, it’s difficult to know who changed a salary, who added an employee, or who approved a payment. Your policy must divide this work into three steps: Step 1: Preparation (HR Admin) Gathers the raw data, logs the overtime hours, and updates new onboarding profiles. Step 2: Review (Finance Manager) Double-checks the calculations, confirms tax tiers, and cross-references the master budget. Step 3: Approval (CFO/Founder): Approves and locks down the monthly run. Protect your business by using strict role-based access in your software to build solid payroll controls. Eazipay has a feature called roles and permissions that gives access to one owner who eventually brings the right team as part of the payroll work and every process update is documented clearly. HR staff should only edit basic employee details and involve the right HR associates, while accountants handle financial fields and involve the right financial associates when required. Locking these permissions prevents unauthorized changes, keeps responsibility clear as the business grows and ensures nothing is modified without passing through the official payroll approval process. Managing Statutory and Other Payroll Deductions Mistakes in remittances lead to penalties in Nigeria. Your policy must outline exact calculation rules and monthly deadlines to follow: Pay-As-You-Earn (PAYE) Tax: You must deduct personal income tax from your staff and pay it to the State Internal Revenue Service where they live. These tax rates must follow the official rules set by the Nigeria Revenue Service (NRS). Pension Contributions: Under the Pension Reform Act, you must run a mandatory monthly split, usually 10% from the employer and 8% from the employee. These funds must go to registered Pension Fund Administrators following the rules managed by the National Pension Commission (PenCom). National Housing Fund (NHF): If your team qualifies, a specific percentage of their basic salary must be deducted and paid monthly toward federal housing plans, following the framework run by the Federal Mortgage Bank of Nigeria (FMBN). Beyond these laws, your policy should set clear caps on other deductions like salary advances so employees always take home a fair wage. Handling Payroll Errors, Corrections and Employee Disputes Even with good software, mistakes happen. An allowance may be missed or a tax rate miscalculated if not properly documented. When an employee spots an issue on their payslip, they need to know how to get it fixed calmly. Your salary payment policy should follow a simple, fast timeline: Flag it: The employee emails HR within 5 days of payday. Check it: The payroll admin checks the records and confirms the error. Fix it: If they were underpaid, you send a supplementary transfer within 48 hours, or add it to the next month if they prefer. Every single fix must create a clear digital audit trail so your books stay totally clean. Payroll Data, Records and Confidentiality Your payroll records hold sensitive information; bank accounts, home addresses, and base salaries. If this data leaks, it harms office morale and violates privacy standards. Include these rules in your policy: Only designated HR and finance leaders get access to master payroll files. Make strong passwords and multi-factor authentication (MFA) mandatory on all accounting software. articles.summary: Key Takeaways Only 38% of B2B firms turn 90%-plus of invoiced revenue into cash within 30 days, according to Atradius data. The revenue-cash gap separates revenue booked in your ledger from cash collected and reconciled. That is where working capital gets stuck. Late payments cost firms an average of 3.8% of revenue. For a mid-sized company, that represents roughly $18 million in lost growth. ASC 606 and IFRS 15 tie revenue recognition to the transfer of control. Earned revenue and received cash therefore diverge by design. A SaaS company with a $36,000 annual contract recognizes $3,000 monthly, regardless of when the customer pays. When recognized revenue outpaces collections, hiring, R&D, and marketing spending can stall until cash arrives.
